title: The definite article al-
body: Add الـ to make a noun definite. Before sun letters, the l sound assimilates into the next consonant; spelling keeps the lam. Before moon letters, pronounce the l. The sun letters are ت ث د ذ ر ز س ش ص ض ط ظ ل ن.

title: Gender & plurals
body: Many feminine nouns end in ة, but gender must be learned with each noun. Sound masculine plurals often end in ـون or ـين, and sound feminine plurals in ـات. Broken plurals change the internal pattern and should be learned individually.

title: Personal & attached pronouns
body: أنا، أنتَ، أنتِ، هو، هي، نحن mean I, you masculine, you feminine, he, she, we. Attached pronouns can mark possession: ـي my, ـكَ your masculine, ـكِ your feminine, ـهُ his, ـها her. Some word endings change when suffixes attach.

title: Nominal sentences
body: MSA normally has no spoken equivalent of am/is/are in affirmative present nominal sentences. A definite subject can be followed by an indefinite predicate. Compare the noun phrase the new house with the sentence the house is new.

title: Idafa: belonging together
body: In an idafa, two nouns express a relationship. The first noun takes neither al- nor tanwin. The second noun is in the genitive in fully inflected MSA. Definiteness comes from the second noun or an attached pronoun.

title: Adjective agreement
body: An adjective usually follows its noun and agrees in gender, number, definiteness, and case. Nonhuman plurals commonly take feminine singular agreement. Learn this rule with short paired phrases.

title: Past tense patterns
body: The dictionary form of an Arabic verb is typically third-person masculine singular past, such as كَتَبَ, he wrote. Past-tense person markers attach to the end. Root and stem patterns matter; weak and doubled verbs need separate study.

title: Present tense patterns
body: Present-tense forms use prefixes and sometimes suffixes. From كَتَبَ: يَكْتُبُ he writes, أَكْتُبُ I write, نَكْتُبُ we write. The stem vowel is not always predictable. Learn present and past together.

title: Negation
body: لا commonly negates the present indicative. ما can negate the past. لم before a jussive verb gives past negation; لن before a subjunctive verb marks future negation. ليس negates many nominal sentences.

title: Asking questions
body: هل starts many yes/no questions. Question words include مَن who, ما what, أين where, متى when, كيف how, لماذا why, and كم how much/many.

title: Numbers & counting
body: Arabic number agreement is a full topic of its own. One and two generally agree with the noun; three to ten show gender polarity and usually take a plural counted noun in the genitive. The numbers deck teaches standalone forms, not every number–noun combination.

title: The dual
body: Two of something can be marked on the noun itself: ـان in the nominative and ـين in the accusative or genitive. ة becomes ت before the dual ending. Dual forms also appear in pronouns and verbs.

title: Dates, months & dialects
body: This track uses Modern Standard Arabic. Gregorian month names vary by region: January is يناير in Egypt and many Gulf contexts, and كانون الثاني in much of the Levant. June: يونيو / حزيران. July: يوليو / تموز. Hijri months form a separate lunar calendar; do not substitute them for Gregorian months.

title: Vowels & special letters
body: Fatha َ is short a, kasra ِ short i, damma ُ short u. Sukun ْ marks no vowel; shadda ّ doubles a consonant. Tanwin ً ٍ ٌ adds an n sound in inflected contexts. ا و ي can mark long aa, uu, ii. Hamza ء is a glottal stop; ة is ta marbuta, and ى is alef maqsura.
